opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really hard question, and I'm pretty uncertain. My overall picture is that if you just keep scaling up models like GPT-4, so more compute, more data, maybe some improvements in how we train them, there's a reasonable chance you get to something that can do most of the cognitive work humans do. But I don't think it's a sure thing, and I think the timelines are wide.

One way I approach it is to look at the trend lines we have. Going from GPT-2 to GPT-3 to GPT-4, each roughly one or two orders of magnitude in effective compute, you see these qualitative jumps in what the models can do. Then you ask how many more orders of magnitude you'd need before these systems are as useful as a human worker across a broad range of tasks. If you extrapolate naively, it doesn't look crazy that a few more orders of magnitude, combined with algorithmic progress, could get you there. Maybe that's something like a decade. But there's a lot of uncertainty about how those loss improvements translate into actual competence on long, messy, real-world tasks.

I think the biggest open question is less about raw knowledge or short-horizon reasoning, where these models are already quite impressive, and more about whether they can do sustained, autonomous work. Can a model pursue a goal over days or weeks, notice when it's gone wrong, recover, and coordinate with other agents? Humans are very good at learning on the job and adapting. Current models are much weaker there. It's possible scale plus fine-tuning, RL on longer-horizon tasks, and better scaffolding closes that gap. It's also possible you hit diminishing returns and need some deeper conceptual change.

If you forced me to put numbers on it, I'd say something like a 15 percent chance that we have AI systems capable of replacing most human cognitive labor by 2030, and maybe 40 percent by 2040. I hold those loosely. And the thing I'd emphasize is that you don't need full replacement for this to matter enormously. Once AI meaningfully accelerates AI research itself, things could move much faster than a simple extrapolation would suggest. That's part of why I think it's worth taking the possibility seriously now, and why I spend so much time worrying about whether we'll understand and be able to control these systems when we get there.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I'm pretty uncertain, and I'd put real probability on a few different stories.

One story is that you just keep scaling. You take the current recipe, you make the models bigger, you train them on more data, you add a bit more RL on top, and you get something that can do most of what a human knowledge worker does. I don't think that's crazy. If you'd asked me ten years ago whether GPT-4 was possible with this little architectural insight, I would have been fairly skeptical, and I was wrong. So I've updated toward "the simple thing keeps working" more than I would have liked.

But I think there are a couple of reasons to hedge. One is that the kind of work GPT-4 is good at is work where you have a lot of relevant text on the internet, and where a task can be done in a single pass without much long-horizon planning or learning on the job. A lot of human cognitive labor isn't like that. It involves picking up a new codebase over weeks, noticing when your approach isn't working, and adjusting. It's not obvious that scaling the pretraining objective buys you that for free. It might. There's an argument that longer-horizon competence emerges as a byproduct of predicting humans who do have it. But I'd guess you need something extra, whether that's much more RL, better scaffolding, or new ideas about how models learn from their own experience.

The other reason to hedge is just cost. Each order of magnitude is expensive, and at some point you're limited by data and compute in ways that aren't purely a matter of will. So even if scaling works in principle, the question of whether it works on the timescale of, say, five years versus fifteen depends on things like how much you can squeeze out of synthetic data and algorithmic efficiency.

If I had to put rough numbers on it, I'd say something like a third chance that systems that can broadly substitute for human cognitive labor arrive in the next decade or so without much that would look like a fundamental new idea, and a lot of the remaining mass spread over longer timelines where you needed one or two more ingredients. I think the thing I'm most confident about is that the current trajectory makes the question "will this happen eventually" a lot less interesting than "how fast, and how prepared are we when it does."

astra-6.text:
I think it’s quite plausible that you can get there by scaling up systems that look broadly like GPT-4. I’m much less confident that you can get there just by making the model larger and training it on more text, with everything else held fixed.

There’s a distinction between being able to answer a question and being able to do someone’s job. Doing a job involves pursuing an objective over time, noticing when you’ve made a mistake, gathering additional information, and checking whether the thing you produced actually works. Current models have some of those capabilities, but they don’t put them together reliably enough to substitute for a human across a long task.

The big question is whether those deficiencies are things that improve smoothly as models get better, or whether they require some additional ideas. My guess is that you’ll need additional work, especially on training systems to carry out tasks and learn from the results. But that work could be relatively straightforward. It needn’t involve a fundamentally new approach to AI.

So I wouldn’t look at GPT-4 and say, ‘This is obviously missing something that puts human-level performance out of reach.’ But I also wouldn’t take its performance on short tasks and extrapolate directly to replacing human cognitive labor. A lot depends on how hard it is to turn that underlying competence into reliable behavior over longer periods.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s plausible that the basic approach gets us there, but I’m pretty uncertain about how much is missing. There’s a difference between a system that can answer a difficult question and a system you can hand a job to, have it work for a week, and trust that it will notice mistakes, recover from them, and deliver something useful.

Scaling could improve all of those things. But I wouldn’t assume that you just make GPT-4 larger and suddenly it can do every remote job. You probably also need to train systems to carry out longer tasks, use tools, and check their work. The question is whether those are relatively straightforward extensions of what we’re doing now or whether they expose problems that require substantially new ideas.

My guess is that we should take the possibility of relatively straightforward extensions very seriously. I don’t think we have strong evidence that there’s some fundamental obstacle between the current approach and systems that can do most human cognitive work. But that leaves a huge amount of uncertainty about the timeline and the resources required.
